newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian presidential hopefuls clash in TV debate.
newsitem.headline: Romanian presidential hopefuls clash in TV debate.

text.p: President Ion Iliescu, seeking re-election after seven years in power, fought off attacks by his centrist challenger on corruption and the future of market reforms in their first head-to-head television debate.

Iliescu, a former communist, went on the offensive after opening up a four percentage point lead in the election's first round this month against centrist Emil Constantinescu. He said his rival wanted to reinstate Romania's exiled king and return property to pre-war landlords.

But in 90 minutes of largely uninspiring discussion on Monday night, Iliescu countered accusations that he had failed to tackle corrupt officials, remedy an energy crisis and draw up an affordable programme to improve living standards.
"Why in the past seven years wasn't a single case of corruption brought to a conclusion?" the bearded Constantinescu asked the president in the first of a series of debates.
"That makes Romania the only country in the world where corruption exists but no one is guilty of it."

Iliescu, who came to power in the aftermath of the 1989 upheaval which unseated dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, replied that he had sacked two prosecutors and purged his own Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) of suspect elements.
But Constantinescu said such changes had achieved little and he accused Iliescu of dismissing one minister only after the press had presented incriminating evidence against him.

The president said a programme proposed by Constantinescu's Democratic Convention to cut taxes, improve social benefits, and reduce the growing gap with other east European states like Poland and Hungary was unworkable. It would cost the public purse the equivalent of $1.45 billion per year, he alleged.
Constantinescu said a plan sponsored by Iliescu's ruling party cost more than three times that amount. Iliescu winced and said he would have to check the figures.
Iliescu's PDSR was trounced by the CDR in parliamentary elections also held earlier this month, pushing the party out of government for the first time in the post-communist era.
Iliescu and most members of the outgoing government created a safety net for themselves by winning parliamentary seats.

Constantinescu has been bouyed in the run-off by support from former Prime Minister Petre Roman, third-place finisher in the opening round. Both men say Iliescu must be defeated to end once and for all the communist legacy in Romania.

Political analysts say the president has been deserted in the run-off by most of his erstwhile allies. The leader of one major nationalist group, previously allied with Iliescu's party, accused him on Monday of "lies and diversion" in the campaign.
Iliescu's recent campaign videos have warned workers and farmers that by electing Constantinescu they could lose their land and have the factories where they worked shut down.
But these appeared to have been withdrawn on Monday in favour of shots of Iliescu shaking hands with U.S. President Bill Clinton and attending European Union meetings.
Constantinescu also appeared to catch the president off guard with a final debate question -- did he believe in God?

"I was baptised in the Romanian Orthodox church but during my intellectual development there have been certain changes," Iliescu replied. "But I am still imbued with the basic ideas of christian morality. I am much more Christian than many others who use this for campaign purposes."
